opus-5.5.text:
Suturing is a beautiful example of something that looks simple and is incredibly hard. A surgeon does it almost without thinking, but when you break it down for a robot, every piece is a research problem.

The first issue is deformable materials. Most robotics grew up handling rigid objects: you pick up a block and you know its shape, and its shape doesn't change. Tissue is soft. When you push a needle into it, it bends, stretches and moves away from you. The thread is also deformable, and thread is notoriously hard to model. It can loop, tangle and kink, and its configuration space is essentially infinite-dimensional. Simulating that accurately enough to plan with is still very difficult.

The second issue is perception. In surgery you're working in a small, wet, shiny space, with blood, reflections and occlusion. The needle is tiny and curved, and it's often partially hidden by the tissue or by the instrument itself. Just knowing precisely where the needle tip is, in 3D, at every moment, is a serious challenge.

The third issue is the hardware, which people often overlook. Surgical robots like the da Vinci are cable-driven. That's great for making them small and dexterous, but cables stretch, they have hysteresis, and they behave differently depending on their history. So when you command the robot to go to a position, it doesn't quite get there, and the error isn't consistent. A human surgeon compensates naturally because they're watching and adjusting. For an autonomous system, we've had to learn models of those errors and correct for them.

Then there's the handoff. Suturing usually means passing the needle from one gripper to the other and regrasping it in the right orientation. Each of those steps has a small chance of failure, and errors compound. Even if each step is 95% reliable, a long sequence of stitches quickly becomes unreliable.

Finally, there's variability. Every patient is different and every wound is different. A system that works beautifully on a training phantom in the lab may not generalize to real tissue. That's a recurring theme in robotics: we can get impressive demos, but robustness across the long tail of real-world conditions is the hard part.

So I'm optimistic. We've made real progress, and I think we'll see more supervised autonomy, where the robot does subtasks like suturing under a surgeon's oversight. But I'm cautious about people expecting fully autonomous robot surgeons anytime soon. It's a good reminder that the tasks we find easy are often the hardest for robots.

fable-5.1.text:
Oh, suturing is one of my favourite examples, because when you watch a skilled surgeon do it, it looks almost trivial. They pick up the needle, they drive it through the tissue, they pull the thread, they tie a knot. People assume we should have had robots doing this twenty years ago. And yet it's still, to this day, essentially unsolved as an autonomous task.

The first problem is perception. Tissue is wet, it's shiny, it's deformable, it reflects light in ways that confuse cameras. You have blood, you have specular highlights, you have a surgical thread that is thinner than a millimetre and almost the same colour as everything around it. Just tracking where the needle tip is, and where the thread is, in three dimensions, is really hard. We've had graduate students spend entire PhDs on just that piece.

The second problem is that everything you're touching deforms. When you push a needle into tissue, the tissue moves. It stretches, it dimples, it tears if you're not careful. So you can't plan a trajectory in advance and execute it blindly, the way you might with a rigid part in a factory. You have to constantly adjust based on what the tissue is doing, and we don't have good models of how soft tissue behaves. The physics is genuinely difficult. Finite element models exist, but they're slow and they need parameters we don't know for a given patient.

Third is the thread itself. Thread is what we'd call a deformable linear object, and manipulating those is one of the hard open problems in robotics generally. It tangles, it goes slack, it has friction with itself. Tying a knot with two robotic arms, where you have to pass the thread around, pull it tight with the right tension so it doesn't cut through tissue but also doesn't come loose, that requires a kind of dexterity and tactile sensing that current robots mostly lack. Surgeons feel the tension through their fingers. Our robots, like the da Vinci system, actually have no force feedback at all. The surgeon learns to see tension visually, which is remarkable, but a robot doing it autonomously has to infer the same thing from pixels.

And then there's the broader issue I always come back to, which is that the real world is full of variation. Every wound is different, every patient's anatomy is different, and the consequences of error are severe. In a warehouse, if a robot drops a box, you pick it up. In surgery, there is no undo. So the bar for reliability is extraordinarily high, and we're nowhere near it. We've done demonstrations in the lab on phantoms and in some animal studies, and the results are encouraging, but I'd say we're still a long way from a robot that you'd want closing an incision on a person without a surgeon's hands right there.

astra-6.text:
One of the hardest things is that the material keeps changing shape. If you’re assembling a car, you can often assume that a part is rigid and that you know where it is. With tissue, as soon as you touch it or pull on the thread, it deforms. So the robot has to keep observing and adjusting as it goes.

Then there’s the needle. A surgical needle is curved, and you want to drive it through the tissue along that curve, rather than just push it straight in. You have to grasp it at the right orientation, choose where it enters and exits, and control the motion without damaging the tissue.

And the thread is especially challenging. It’s thin, flexible, and can disappear from view or get tangled. You need enough tension to bring the edges of the wound together, but not so much that you tear the tissue. Humans make all these little adjustments almost without thinking. Getting a robot to perceive what’s happening and make those adjustments reliably is a very difficult problem.

sol-6.1.text:
One of the hardest things is that tissue is deformable. If you’re assembling a car, you can often assume that the parts have a fairly fixed shape. With tissue, every time you pull on it or push a needle through it, the geometry changes. So the robot has to keep observing what’s happening and adjust its motions as it goes.

Then there’s the needle itself. It’s curved, and you want to drive it through the tissue along that curve, with the right placement and depth, without causing unnecessary damage. After that, you have to manage the thread, which is flexible, can get tangled, and can be difficult to see. And you need enough tension to bring the edges of the wound together without pulling so hard that you tear the tissue.

So it’s a combination of perception, planning, and very delicate control under uncertainty. A surgeon makes all of those adjustments almost without thinking, but getting a robot to do them reliably is quite challenging.
